moments.title: Wundt opens the first psychology laboratory
moments.body:
Wundt establishes the first laboratory dedicated to experimental psychology in a former dining room. Students measure reaction times to flashing lights and ticking metronomes.

The goal is to separate psychology from philosophy by tying it to stopwatches, calibrated apparatus and trained observers.

quote.text: In psychology, the person looks upon himself as from within.

moments.takeaway: Psychology becomes an experimental discipline when measurement is added to introspection.

moments.title: Watson's behaviourist manifesto
moments.body:
Watson publishes 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It', insisting psychology study only observable behaviour.

The move sidelines introspection and unconscious explanation. American psychology will be dominated by behaviourism for the next four decades.
moments.takeaway: Demanding observability shaped what counted as data in the discipline for forty years.

moments.title: The cognitive revolution
moments.body:
At an MIT symposium and in linked publications, the assumption that minds can be modelled as information-processing systems takes hold.

Miller's 'magical number seven' (1956), Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner, and Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist together reset the field.
moments.takeaway: Treating the mind as a computational system reopened questions behaviourism had closed.

now.title: Psychology today
now.body: Contemporary psychology spans cognitive neuroscience, computational modelling, large-scale replication efforts and clinical practice. The 2010s 'replication crisis' (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) has reshaped methodological standards.
now.open_questions: How robust are foundational findings under preregistration and adversarial collaboration? How should psychological evidence be weighted in policy?

items.reflection: Psychology's history shows recurring swings between observable behaviour and inferred mental processes. Each turn discards some claims and rescues others.

moments.title: Pavlov's digestion research begins
moments.body: Pavlov studies gastric secretion in dogs. His method, surgically isolating digestive juices, will win the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
moments.takeaway: Conditioning research begins as a by-product of physiology, not psychology.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: Pavlov is awarded the prize for digestive physiology, not psychology. The Conditional Reflex work follows over the next two decades.
moments.takeaway: Major figures are often recognised for one set of contributions and remembered for another.

moments.title: Conditioned Reflexes published in English
moments.body:
Anrep's English edition makes Pavlov's full account available to American psychologists, just as behaviourism is consolidating its dominance.

Watson had already invoked Pavlov in his 1913 manifesto.
moments.takeaway: Translation and publication timing shape which ideas reach which audiences.

now.title: Classical conditioning today
now.body: Conditioning paradigms remain central to learning theory, fear research and clinical exposure therapies. Computational models map the neural circuits involved (amygdala, prefrontal cortex).
now.open_questions: How do classical conditioning circuits interact with reinforcement learning models in machine learning?

items.reflection: Pavlov's work is often presented as the start of behaviourism. He himself was a physiologist who resisted that framing.

moments.title: Bowlby's 44 thieves
moments.body:
Bowlby publishes a study of 44 juvenile thieves and 44 controls, arguing maternal separation in early childhood predicts later antisocial behaviour.

The methods, with researcher-conducted interviews and a small sample, would not meet current standards.
moments.takeaway: Foundational studies can frame a field's questions while using methods later revised.

moments.title: Attachment and Loss volume one
moments.body:
Bowlby integrates ethology, evolutionary biology and clinical observation into a developmental theory of attachment.

The distinction between privation and deprivation will be sharpened by Michael Rutter (1981).
moments.takeaway: Cross-disciplinary integration produced a theory that outlived its original methods.

moments.title: Patterns of Attachment
moments.body:
Ainsworth's book details the Strange Situation procedure and the classifications: secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant.

Main and Solomon (1990) will later add disorganised attachment as a fourth category.
moments.takeaway: Operationalising a theory through a standardised procedure made empirical comparison possible.

now.title: Attachment research today
now.body: Cross-cultural research (van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg, 1988) showed proportions of attachment styles vary by culture. Meta-analyses link disorganised attachment with later mental health outcomes.
now.open_questions: How stable are early classifications into adulthood? How do interventions affect attachment outcomes for at-risk infants?

items.reflection: Bowlby developed his theory while working with children evacuated and bereaved during the Second World War. Historical context shapes which questions get asked.

moments.title: Eichmann on trial in Jerusalem
moments.body: The trial raises questions about how ordinary people participate in atrocity. Arendt later coins 'the banality of evil' (1963).
moments.takeaway: Postwar Europe shaped the questions academic psychology then took into the laboratory.

moments.title: Behavioral Study of Obedience
moments.body: Milgram reports that 26 of 40 participants delivered the maximum apparent shock under an experimenter's instruction. He frames the result as a finding about situational power, not personality.

quote.text: Stark authority was pitted against the subjects' strongest moral imperatives.

moments.takeaway: Situational pressure produced obedience far beyond expert and lay predictions.

moments.title: Burger's partial replication
moments.body:
Under modified ethical protocols, Burger obtains broadly similar obedience rates to a 150-volt cut-off point.

Later archival work (Perry, 2013) reopens questions about Milgram's data handling.
moments.takeaway: Even classic findings continue to be re-examined against new evidence.

now.title: Obedience research today
now.body: Modern variants use immersive virtual reality (Slater et al., 2006) to test responses without ethical violations. Meta-research focuses on individual differences and dissent dynamics.
now.open_questions: What conditions reliably increase resistance to harmful authority? How do online environments mediate similar dynamics?

items.reflection: Milgram's studies could not be run today. Their continued teaching depends on context about both their power and their costs.

moments.title: Syntactic Structures
moments.body:
Chomsky argues language could not be learned by reinforcement of word combinations because speakers produce sentences they have never heard.

He proposes generative grammar as a model of competence.
moments.takeaway: Productivity of language posed a problem behaviourist learning theory could not solve.

moments.title: Review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior
moments.body:
Chomsky's critique of Skinner's Verbal Behavior (1957) argues operant conditioning cannot account for syntactic productivity.

The review is widely credited with shifting the centre of psycholinguistics.
moments.takeaway: A single review can mark a generational turn in a discipline.

moments.title: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
moments.body: Chomsky introduces the distinction between competence and performance and the idea of an innate Language Acquisition Device.
moments.takeaway: Nativist assumptions about language structure shaped cognitive science for decades.

now.title: Language and mind today
now.body: Large language models challenge some nativist claims about productivity. Statistical learning research (Saffran et al., 1996) shows infants extract structure from input. The debate over what is innate vs learned continues.
now.open_questions: What does the success of statistical language models say about innateness? How do bilingual brains organise multiple grammars?

items.reflection: Chomsky's critique demolished one paradigm but installed another whose own empirical commitments are now under review.

moments.title: Wundt opens the Leipzig laboratory
moments.body: Wundt establishes the first laboratory dedicated to experimental psychology in a former dining room at the University of Leipzig. He trains graduate students from across Europe and the US in calibrated apparatus, reaction-time measurement, and 'trained introspection' under controlled conditions.

quote.text: In psychology, the person looks upon himself as from within.

moments.takeaway: Psychology becomes a discipline distinct from philosophy at the moment it adopts the laboratory.

moments.title: The Wundt diaspora
moments.body: By 1900, Wundt had supervised around 180 doctoral dissertations. His students included G. Stanley Hall (founded the first US psychology laboratory at Johns Hopkins, 1883), Edward Titchener (Cornell, structuralism), Hugo Münsterberg, James McKeen Cattell.
moments.takeaway: A single laboratory's training shaped the formation of psychology departments across two continents in two decades.

now.title: Wundt's legacy
now.body: Reaction time methodology is foundational to modern cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience (e.g., Stroop task, lexical decision tasks). The introspective methods Wundt championed were sidelined by behaviourism but have returned in subjective reports paired with brain imaging.
now.open_questions: What is the role of first-person reports in a brain-based psychology? Phenomenology and consciousness studies are still finding their footing.

items.reflection: Most disciplines have founding myths. Psychology's founding moment is unusually well-documented and unusually instrumental — a single room, a single set of stopwatches, training a generation.

moments.title: James's Harvard laboratory
moments.body: James sets up a small laboratory at Harvard for psychological demonstrations — contested as either the first or among the earliest in the US. He is more philosopher than experimentalist by temperament.
moments.takeaway: American psychology begins as a hybrid of philosophy and physiology.

moments.title: The Principles of Psychology
moments.body: Twelve years in the writing, James's 'Principles' covers the stream of consciousness, habit, emotion (the James-Lange theory), self, will. The book defines what psychology can and should address. James himself disliked teaching it: 'A loathsome, distended, tumefied, bloated, dropsical mass.'

quote.text: Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent.

moments.takeaway: American psychology's foundational textbook frames the subject for a generation.

now.title: Pragmatism today
now.body: James's pragmatism (1907) and emphasis on functional consequences of mental states resonates with modern cognitive science and ecological psychology. The stream of consciousness concept influenced literature (Joyce, Woolf) as much as psychology.
now.open_questions: What is consciousness 'for' functionally? The hard problem James named is still open.

items.reflection: James was sceptical of his own discipline's overreach. His acknowledgment that psychology might never become a strict science remains a useful corrective to disciplinary overconfidence.

moments.title: The Interpretation of Dreams
moments.body: Freud publishes 'Die Traumdeutung' (dated 1900 but printed November 1899). The book argues that dreams are wish-fulfilments expressing unconscious desires, accessible through symbolic interpretation. Sales were initially poor (600 copies in eight years) but the book founded psychoanalysis as a movement.
moments.takeaway: A book that didn't sell became one of the most influential works of the 20th century.

moments.title: Clark University lectures
moments.who: Freud, Jung, Ferenczi visit the US
moments.body: Freud delivers five lectures at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, at the invitation of G. Stanley Hall. The lectures introduce psychoanalysis to a major American audience.
moments.takeaway: American psychology absorbed Freud's ideas selectively; psychoanalysis became influential in psychiatry and culture more than in academic psychology.

now.title: Freud after Freud
now.body: Academic psychology has largely moved beyond Freud's specific theories, which were not testable in the modern sense. His broader claims — that much of mental life is not consciously accessible, that early experience shapes adult psychology, that defense mechanisms operate — have found partial support in cognitive psychology, attachment research, and trauma studies. The clinical influence remains substantial in psychodynamic therapy.
now.open_questions: How much of Freud's insight survives empirical examination? The answer is 'less than he claimed but more than zero'.

items.reflection: Freud is the rare figure whose work shaped 20th-century literature, art and politics as much as his discipline. Academic psychology's relationship with his legacy is uneasy: dismissed as unfalsifiable, kept as a historical reference, reread occasionally as cognitive science rediscovers unconscious processing.

moments.title: The Behavior of Organisms
moments.body: Skinner publishes 'The Behavior of Organisms', detailing operant conditioning. The 'operant chamber' (popularly the Skinner box) allows precise measurement of how reinforcement schedules shape behaviour. Schedules of reinforcement (fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, variable-interval) produce reliable patterns.
moments.takeaway: Behaviour can be shaped by environmental contingencies — and measured to a precision other branches of psychology envied.

moments.title: Walden Two to Beyond Freedom and Dignity
moments.body: Skinner extends his vision to social organisation. Walden Two (1948) imagines a behaviourist utopia. Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971) argues 'autonomous man' is an unhelpful fiction. The book attracts both intense interest and intense criticism.
moments.takeaway: Behavioural science as a vision for social engineering — controversial then, with echoes now in 'nudge' and behavioural design.

now.title: Operant conditioning today
now.body: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is used in education and clinical settings (notably autism intervention, where it is also controversial). Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules underpin slot machines and many engagement features of social media platforms. The basic principles remain robust; the ethical applications continue to be debated.
now.open_questions: What is the boundary between using behavioural principles for the user's benefit and for an institution's?

items.reflection: Skinner's empirical work was meticulous; his philosophical extension was sweeping. Both have outlasted the strict behaviourism of his time.

moments.title: Forty-Four Juvenile Thieves
moments.who: John Bowlby, London Child Guidance Clinic
moments.body: Bowlby's study of 44 juvenile thieves and 44 controls argues that 'affectionless psychopathy' correlates with maternal separation in early childhood. The study has methodological limitations (interviews conducted by the clinician), but the framing question — does early relational disruption shape later behaviour? — sets a research agenda.
moments.takeaway: Clinical observation generates the hypothesis that decades of subsequent work refine.

moments.title: Maternal Care and Mental Health
moments.body: Bowlby's WHO report on the mental health of homeless children synthesises wartime evidence on orphans and evacuees. It argues for the importance of continuous early care. The report shaped postwar attitudes to maternal employment and institutional care in ways that exceeded the evidence.
moments.takeaway: Policy uptake of psychological research can outrun what the research strictly supports.

moments.title: Attachment and Loss trilogy
moments.body: Bowlby integrates ethology (Lorenz's imprinting work), evolutionary biology and clinical observation into Attachment (1969), Separation (1973) and Loss (1980). The theoretical framework is mature when Mary Ainsworth (his collaborator from the 1950s) operationalises it through the Strange Situation.
moments.takeaway: A theory that drew on a wider intellectual base than typical mid-century psychology proved more durable.

now.title: Attachment today
now.body: Attachment theory has been extended to adult romantic relationships (Hazan & Shaver, 1987), to clinical practice (Attachment-Based Family Therapy), and to neuroscience of social bonding. Cross-cultural research has refined the original claims; the broad framework remains influential.
now.open_questions: How modifiable are attachment patterns through intervention? Some evidence for plasticity into adulthood; the specific routes remain studied.

items.reflection: Bowlby worked through the Second World War's mass displacement of children. The historical context shaped which questions felt urgent — and shaped policy responses that the theory itself didn't strictly entail.

moments.title: Cognitive revolution year
moments.body: Several pivotal events in one year: George Miller's 'Magical Number Seven' paper (March); Allen Newell and Herbert Simon demonstrate Logic Theorist at the Dartmouth AI Workshop (summer); Noam Chomsky presents 'Three Models of Language' at MIT's Symposium on Information Theory (September); Bruner, Goodnow & Austin publish 'A Study of Thinking'.
moments.takeaway: A cluster of independent developments crystallised the information-processing approach to mind.

moments.title: Chomsky's review of Skinner
moments.body: Chomsky's devastating review of Skinner's 'Verbal Behavior' (Language, 1959) argues that productivity of language cannot be explained by operant conditioning. The review marks the moment behaviourism's claim to explain everything becomes untenable.
moments.takeaway: A single 31-page review changed the centre of gravity of an entire discipline.

moments.title: Cognitive Psychology textbook
moments.body: Neisser's textbook 'Cognitive Psychology' gives the field a name and consolidates the new approach. The information-processing metaphor — mind as computer — becomes dominant.
moments.takeaway: A textbook canonises what had been a loose collection of researchers.

now.title: Cognitive science today
now.body: The information-processing approach gave way to embodied, embedded, situated cognition in some quarters; rejoined neuroscience in others (cognitive neuroscience from the 1990s). Modern cognitive science includes computational modelling, fMRI, behavioural experiments and philosophy of mind. Large language models have revived debates Chomsky's review seemed to settle.
now.open_questions: What does the success of statistical language models tell us about the structure of human language and cognition?

items.reflection: Paradigm shifts in psychology often look in retrospect like a single year. Up close, they were the consolidation of work done over decades by people who weren't sure where it was going.

moments.title: DSM-I published
moments.body: The first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual covers 106 disorders, heavily influenced by psychoanalytic concepts. Homosexuality is listed as a sociopathic personality disturbance.
moments.takeaway: Psychiatric classification began as a frame that reflected its era's assumptions.

moments.title: Homosexuality declassified
moments.who: APA board, after activist pressure and the Rosenhan experiment
moments.body: After campaigns by gay rights activists and increasing professional doubt, the APA removes homosexuality from DSM-II. Robert Spitzer's role in driving the change was central. David Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' (Science, 1973) had highlighted diagnostic unreliability.
moments.takeaway: Diagnostic categories can be revised as social attitudes and evidence shift.

moments.title: DSM-III shifts to operationalised criteria
moments.body: DSM-III moves to explicit diagnostic criteria for each disorder, modelling reliability rather than aetiology. The descriptive approach replaces the psychodynamic framing. PTSD enters the manual.
moments.takeaway: Reliability improves at the cost of theoretical depth — a deliberate trade-off.

moments.title: DSM-5 maintains the categorical framework
moments.body: DSM-5 makes incremental changes (autism spectrum, gender dysphoria, removal of grief exclusion for major depression) but preserves the categorical structure. NIMH's RDoC initiative (announced 2013) signals a research push toward dimensional alternatives.
moments.takeaway: Operational structure has been remarkably stable; clinical realities and research evidence have changed around it.

now.title: Classification today
now.body: ICD-11 (WHO, 2022) includes some dimensional elements (especially for personality disorders). HiTOP (Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, 2017) offers a structured dimensional alternative. Categorical diagnosis persists because insurance, research and clinical communication require labels.
now.open_questions: Can dimensional and categorical approaches coexist clinically? Most modern frameworks try to hybrid.

items.reflection: Classification systems carry the assumptions of their era. The history of the DSM is partly a history of what each generation considered worth pathologising.

moments.title: Beck develops cognitive therapy
moments.who: Aaron T. Beck, University of Pennsylvania
moments.body: Beck, trained as a psychoanalyst, notices that depressed patients have automatic negative thoughts about themselves, the world and the future ('cognitive triad'). He develops cognitive therapy, focusing on identifying and challenging these thoughts. Albert Ellis had developed Rational Emotive Therapy in parallel from 1955.
moments.takeaway: Clinical observation by a working psychoanalyst yields a new therapy.

moments.title: Cognitive Therapy of Depression
moments.body: The book sets out cognitive therapy for depression as a structured, short-term, manualised approach. Randomised trials in the 1970s-80s show comparable efficacy to antidepressants for many patients.
moments.takeaway: Cognitive therapy becomes one of the first psychotherapies with structured efficacy evidence.

moments.title: Cognitive-behavioural integration
moments.who: Beck and others integrate with behavioural therapy
moments.body: Combined cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) integrates Beck's cognitive techniques with behavioural activation, exposure and skills training. It becomes the dominant evidence-based psychotherapy through the 1990s.
moments.takeaway: Integration of complementary techniques produces a more flexible therapeutic approach.

now.title: CBT today
now.body: CBT is the most-researched psychotherapy; NICE guidelines recommend it for many conditions. UK's IAPT programme (2008) made CBT widely available. Third-wave variants (DBT for borderline personality, ACT for chronic conditions, mindfulness-based approaches) extend the framework. Routine outcomes data show effectiveness in real-world conditions, though smaller than RCT effects.
now.open_questions: Is CBT effective because of its specific techniques or because of common therapy factors (alliance, hope)? Dismantling studies have produced mixed answers.

items.reflection: Beck died in 2021 aged 100, having seen his clinical innovation become one of the most-used psychotherapies in the world. The arc from observation to manualised treatment to evidence-based default took 60 years.

moments.title: Bem's precognition paper triggers methodological scrutiny
moments.body: Bem publishes 'Feeling the Future' in JPSP, claiming evidence for precognition — extra-sensory perception of future events. The paper used standard psychology methods. Critics including Wagenmakers argued the methods themselves were the problem; if standard practices could produce 'evidence' for the impossible, what did that say about other 'significant' findings?
moments.takeaway: An extraordinary claim made with ordinary methods exposed the ordinariness of the problem.

moments.title: Reproducibility Project: Psychology
moments.who: Open Science Collaboration, led by Brian Nosek
moments.body: 270 researchers attempted to replicate 100 published psychology findings. 36% replicated; effect sizes were on average about half the originals. The Science paper became one of the most-cited psychology papers of the decade.
moments.takeaway: A coordinated test of the field's published findings produced uncomfortable but actionable results.

moments.title: Methodological reform
moments.body: Preregistration, registered reports, the OSF (Open Science Framework, 2013), badges for open data, the TOP guidelines (2014). Many landmark findings — ego depletion, power posing, the marshmallow test as a predictor of life outcomes — have been substantially revised or weakened on replication.
moments.takeaway: The reforms haven't fully fixed the field but have changed publishing norms across leading psychology journals.

now.title: Open science today
now.body: Preregistration is increasingly default for confirmatory studies. Registered reports appear in over 300 journals. Massive collaborations (the Many Labs projects, Psychological Science Accelerator) enable replication at scale. Adversarial collaborations (e.g., Kahneman-style) test specific claims with both sides' methods. The crisis has spread beyond psychology to medicine, economics and machine learning.
now.open_questions: How robust are findings being produced now? The reforms are improving quality but the pipeline is long; full effects on published literature will take decades.

items.reflection: The replication crisis is a story of a discipline correcting itself, painfully and incompletely. Other fields are at earlier stages of the same realisation.
